title: Genesis 25. The Cup of Generations.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 25. The Cup of Generations.
Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah.
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Six sons.
The man whose wife was barren for ninety years now has six more children after Sarah's death.
But the text does not linger.
It lists the sons, lists their sons, and moves on.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.
To the sons of the concubines, Abraham gave gifts.
While he still lived, he sent them away from Isaac his son,
eastward, to the east country.
The same pattern as Ishmael.
The Cup of promise is separated from every other cup.
The sons who are not the covenant are blessed with gifts and sent away.
The vessel that holds the promise narrows again,
from Abraham to Isaac alone.
These are the days of the years of Abraham's life which he lived:
one hundred seventy-five years.
Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age,
an old man and full of years,
and was gathered to his people.
Old and full.
Not the drumbeat of chapter five, and he died.
Not the flat repetition of years and deaths.
Full.
The man who left Ur with nothing, who was promised everything,
who believed and was counted righteous,
who laughed and lied and bargained and built altars and offered his son and bought a grave and planted a tamarisk,
is gathered to his people.
The Cup that was carried for a hundred and seventy-five years is set down.
Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah,
in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite,
which is near Mamre.
The field which Abraham purchased from the children of Heth.
Abraham was buried there with Sarah his wife.
The brothers who were separated stand together at their father's grave.
The son of the promise and the son of the arrangement.
Isaac, who was nearly offered on Moriah.
Ishmael,
who was sent into the wilderness with bread and a skin of water.
They meet at the cave.
The Cup that was given to one and blessed upon the other is now held by both as they lower their father into the ground beside Sarah.
The first time the two cups are in the same place since the day Hagar was sent away.
After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac, his son.
Isaac lived by Beer-lahai-roi,
the well of the Living One who sees me.
The blessing passes.
The Cup moves from Abraham to Isaac.
And Isaac lives at the well,
the well Hagar named when God saw her in the wilderness.
The son of the promise dwells at the well of the woman who was cast out.
The God who sees is still seeing.
Then the text turns to Ishmael.
These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian,
Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham.
Twelve sons.
Twelve princes, according to their nations.
Exactly what God promised in chapter seventeen: I will make him fruitful.
I will multiply him exceedingly.
He shall father twelve princes.
I will make him a great nation.
God kept His word.
To the son who was not the promise.
To the son who was cast out.
The Cup of arrangement was blessed, sent away, and became twelve nations.
The God who was not consulted in the arrangement was faithful to the arrangement's fruit.
Ishmael lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
He breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people.
They lived from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt,
as you go toward Assyria.
He settled over against all his kinsmen.
Over against.
The same word from chapter sixteen,
the wild donkey who dwells over against all his kinsmen.
The son who was separated lives separated.
But he is gathered to his people.
He dies.
He is buried.
He is not forgotten.
Then the text turns to Isaac.
This is the history of the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son.
Abraham fathered Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah,
the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Paddan-aram,
the sister of Laban the Syrian, to be his wife.
Twenty years.
Isaac married Rebekah at forty.
The next event is when he is sixty.
Twenty years of marriage.
Twenty years of the Cup in a tent with a womb that is closed.
The same pattern as Abraham and Sarah,
the promise held by a barren woman.
Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren.
The father who did not intercede for Sodom,
who did not bargain with God, who did not speak on Moriah,
prays.
The man who was silent on the mountain opens his mouth in the tent.
And the Lord was entreated by him.
Rebekah conceived.
The man who was offered prays for the womb that is closed.
The son who was bound on the altar intercedes for the child who is not yet conceived.
The Cup that was nearly emptied now asks to be filled.
And God answers.
But what God answers is not peace.
The children struggled together within her.
She said: If it is like this, why do I live?
She went to inquire of the Lord.
The same word used for the struggle of the flood,
the crushing of the deep.
The children crush each other inside the womb.
The Cup that was prayed for arrives as conflict.
The promise that was sought in prayer produces violence before it produces breath.
The Lord said to her: Two nations are in your womb.
Two peoples shall be divided from your body.
The one people shall be stronger than the other.
The older shall serve the younger.
The Cup of generations passes, but it divides.
Two in the womb.
Already struggling.
Already at war before they are born.
The promise that narrowed from Abraham to Isaac now narrows from Isaac to one of two.
And the word God speaks before they are born reverses the order:
the older shall serve the younger.
The Cup that was always given to the first, Cain before Abel,
Ishmael before Isaac, is now promised to the second.
When her days to be delivered were fulfilled,
there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red, all over, like a hairy garment.
They called his name Esau.
After that, his brother came out,
and his hand had hold on Esau's heel.
He was called Jacob.
Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
Red.
Hairy.
Esau, the one who is done, made, handled.
And then Jacob, heel catcher.
The supplanter.
The one who grabs.
The second son comes out of the womb holding the first son's heel.
Before he breathes, he grabs.
Before he sees, he holds.
The Cup that was promised to the younger is held by a hand that was already reaching for the older before birth.
The boys grew.
Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents.
Isaac loved Esau, because he ate of his game.
Rebekah loved Jacob.
The household divides.
The father loves the hunter.
The mother loves the quiet one.
The same fracture as Isaac and Ishmael, one parent favoring one son,
the other favoring the other.
The Cup that was given to a divided womb now sits in a divided tent.
The promise that God said would go to the younger is held in a house where the father prefers the older.
One day, Jacob was cooking stew.
Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted.
He said: Let me eat some of that red stew,
for I am exhausted.
Therefore his name was called Edom, Red.
Jacob said: Sell me your birthright now.
The grabber grabs.
The man who came out holding a heel now demands the heel's prize.
The birthright, the double portion, the inheritance of the firstborn,
the authority of the family, is named in a single word.
And Jacob speaks it before Esau has finished asking for food.
The quiet man in the tent has been waiting.
The stew is not a meal.
It is a transaction.
Esau said: I am about to die.
Of what use is a birthright to me?
The hunter who is exhausted from the field says he is dying.
The man who lives by his strength is undone by hunger.
The same pattern as chapter three, abundance given, desire kindled, boundary crossed.
But here the boundary is not a tree.
It is a birthright.
And the fruit is not forbidden.
It is lentil stew.
Jacob said: Swear to me now.
He swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew.
He ate and drank and rose and went his way.
He ate.
He drank.
He rose.
He went.
Four verbs.
The speed is brutal.
The birthright, the right of the firstborn, the double portion,
the head of the family, the line of the covenant,
is consumed in four verbs.
No ceremony.
No negotiation.
No second thought.
He ate.
He drank.
He rose.
He left.
Thus Esau despised his birthright.
The text does not say Jacob stole it.
It says Esau despised it.
The hunter who was hungry treated the promise as worthless.
The man who lived by the field valued the field's labor above the field's inheritance.
The Cup that was cut in blood, sealed in flesh,
tested on a mountain, sworn by an oath, buried in a grave,
and opened in a tent, is traded for a bowl of lentils.
The Cup of generations, held by Abraham, passed through Isaac,
now dividing between two sons,
sits on a table between a man who sells it and a man who takes it.
The grabber grabs.
The hunter is hungry.
The promise that survived flood and famine and Egypt and Gerar and Moriah is now in the hands of a quiet man who waited until his brother was too tired to care.
The Cup holds.
But the vessel that holds it is not clean.
The hand that reaches for it has been grabbing since before birth.
The promise that God said would go to the younger has arrived,
through a prayer, through a struggle, through a bowl of stew.
Not by faith.
Not by worship.
By taking.
What God said before they were born,
the older shall serve the younger, has happened.
But how it happened is not what God said.
God spoke a promise.
Jacob made a transaction.
The word of God and the grab of a man arrive at the same place by different roads.
And neither road has been walked to its end.
